Title: Untrusted Code & Autonomous Minds: Hardening AI Agent Runtimes on K8s
Description: AI agents now execute real-time code, creating a critical security paradox. How do we enable autonomy without risking breakouts? This session explores "Hardened Runtimes" using Docker Sandboxes, gVisor, and Kata Containers on K8s. We’ll analyze the "Agent-in-the-Box" pattern to decouple reasoning from execution. Learn to orchestrate secure agents in AKS via RuntimeClasses and see a live demo of a sandbox blocking malicious AI-generated code. Security for the age of autonomous minds.
How will your presentation benefit the e: This session bridges the gap between AI innovation and Cloud Native security by leveraging the Docker ecosystem and Kubernetes primitives. As the community shifts toward autonomous agents, many organizations hesitate due to the risks of executing unvalidated code. I provide a production-ready blueprint using Docker Sandboxes, gVisor, and Kata Containers to execute these agents securely. By demonstrating how to maintain OCI standards while hardening runtimes, I empower Platform Engineers to move from "No" to "Yes, safely." This fosters a more resilient, mature, and standardized AI-native infrastructure within the CNCF ecosystem.

Title: Telemetry That Matters
Description: This panel brings together practitioners across open standards, developer experience and real-world reliability engineering. The discussion will examine how zero code instrumentation affects workflows and system understanding, how meaningful telemetry improves day to day engineering work and why unfiltered or unstructured data often has the opposite effect. The conversation will cover practical lessons for filtering, dropping, reducing and shaping telemetry.
How will your presentation benefit the e:
Organizations are transitioning from collecting everything to collecting only what is necessary. This shift requires clear thinking about the intent and value of each telemetry signal across metrics, logs and traces. By combining perspectives from standards design, developer engagement and operational experience, this panel provides a grounded and practical view on how to build sustainable observability practices. Attendees will gain tools to reason about what to instrument, what to keep and what to remove, ensuring that the telemetry they retain genuinely supports developer workflows and system understanding.

Our panel will address the following key discussion points:

• Modern developer experience for instrumentation and where friction still occurs
• Zero code instrumentation and its practical benefits and limitations
• How telemetry quality affects debugging, incident response and MTTR
• Why teams accumulate excessive or low value telemetry and the impact it creates
• Reduction strategies including sampling, cardinality management, data shaping and signal prioritization
• Scaling telemetry collection to fleets of collectors with an OpAMP server
• Approaches to balancing observability coverage with data volume and cost constraints
• Frameworks for evaluating purpose, actionability and necessity of telemetry signals

A minimal dashboard is then used to inspect policy failures, affected namespaces and policy execution duration.

This approach encourages safer policy rollout, easier debugging, and greater confidence in enforcement, while remaining portable across clusters and compatible with other Prometheus-style tooling, contributing to more transparent and operable Kubernetes platforms overall.

Title: Transparent by Design: Shipping Artifacts and Evidence for Supply Chain Security
Description: Secure supply chains create a web of artifacts—images, charts, manifests, SBOMs, signatures, provenance—easy to verify in connected CI, but painful in airgapped or constrained environments where tools, keys, and metadata aren’t reachable. This talk introduces an evidence-first approach: ship artifacts plus the proof and policy to verify them. See how Zarf (OpenSSF Sandbox) uses a declarative, versioned manifest so verification is portable, repeatable, and transparent.
How will your presentation benefit the e:
Transparent, evidence-first delivery benefits the ecosystem by making trust portable and repeatable across organizations, not just within a single CI system. When artifacts ship with their signatures, attestations, SBOMs, and declared verification expectations, downstream consumers can validate provenance and integrity without recreating the producer’s tooling stack or relying on connected-services. 

This reduces fragmentation in how teams implement supply chain controls, improves interoperability between projects and vendors, and raises the baseline for secure-by-default releases. It also strengthens auditability and incident response while enabling adoption in constrained, regulated, and airgapped environments that are often left behind by connectivity-dependent security models.

Title: Observability in the Matrix: Choosing the Right AI Agent to Escape the Chaos
Description: Trapped in a storm of metrics, logs, and traces, you discover the truth: you’re inside the Observability Matrix. In this talk, we explore four AI agents : HolmesGPT, Kagent, Sympozium, and K8sGPT ,each offering a different pill to cut through chaos. Like Neo choosing red or blue, you’ll see how they reveal root causes, reduce noise, enrich signals, and avoid AI‑driven illusions in your Kubernetes world.
How will your presentation benefit the e:
This talk contributes to the cloud-native ecosystem by helping practitioners navigate the growing complexity of AI-driven observability like choosing the right agent to escape the Matrix. As teams adopt tools like HolmesGPT, Kagent, Opni, and K8sGPT, they face a new challenge: distinguishing between meaningful insights and AI-generated noise. By comparing these tools through real-world patterns and use cases, this session lowers the barrier to adoption and helps teams make informed decisions based on context, control, and clarity.
It also strengthens production readiness by exposing the trade-offs of automation, sampling, and signal correlation. Attendees will leave with strategies to build observability stacks that are not only intelligent but also trustworthy reducing blind spots and improving reliability across Kubernetes and CNCF projects.
Finally, the session fosters a shared understanding of AI observability. Instead of siloed experimentation, it encourages teams to think in terms of agent roles, telemetry pipelines, and unified signals promoting collaboration, open standards, and a healthier community culture. Because in the Matrix of cloud-native systems, survival depends not just on seeing the truth but knowing which agent to trust.

Key Takeaways:
- Compare five AI-driven observability tools and their unique strengths
- Understand how each tool handles Kubernetes-specific challenges
- Learn how to avoid common pitfalls in AI-powered telemetry
- Discover best practices for integrating AI into your observability stack
- Leave with a framework for choosing the right “agent” for your team
- Can we observe the agent to understand its efficiency?

Title: From Dev Environment to Production Breach: Developer Access into Supply Chain Breaches
Description: Attackers love developers because their machines hold the keys to the software supply chain. Devs often have cloud creds, CI tokens, SSH keys, and package publishing access. Recent attacks like Nx s1ngularity, Shai-Hulud, and malicious AI agents show how trusted tools can become paths to credential theft and code execution. Let's talk about better securing the developer workstation and some practical ways to reduce your risk of becoming another link in another supply chain attack.
How will your presentation benefit the e: My hope is to help developers, platform engineers, and security practitioners better understand that the developer workstation is an entry point to CI/CD, package registries, infrastructure, and production systems, which is what attackers are after. I will talk about open source and free tools that developers can leverage for local work, vs when enterprise tooling is likely required.  Improving secure development habits, strengthening software supply chain resilience, and helping stop these attacks from propagating.

Title: Assume Breach: Mapping the OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten to Containment, Not Just Prevention
Description: The OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten is the community's most cited security framework, but most teams use it only as a prevention checklist. This talk flips the model: for 6 of the 10 risks, containment beats prevention. We'll walk through K01, K05, K07, and K08 (the cluster-to-cloud chain), and give attendees a complete layered security stack they can map their tooling against. Honest, framework-grounded, vendor-agnostic
How will your presentation benefit the e: The OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten is a public, community-maintained framework. This talk helps the broader community get more value from that framework by adding the "assume breach" lens that is often missing from how it is taught. Attendees leave with a complete, layered security stack (identity, policy, secrets, network, isolation, observability) mapped to the OWASP risks, something they can use immediately to audit their own posture and identify gaps.

Title: Zero Trust for APIs: From Edge to Mesh with Istio
Description:
Securing APIs at the edge gateway is standard practice, but what happens once that traffic enters your cluster? Too often, internal networks are treated as trusted zones, leaving service-to-service communication vulnerable. This session tackles that security gap head-on, demonstrating how to build a true Zero Trust network for your APIs using Istio.

We will move beyond perimeter security and implement a defense-in-depth strategy directly within the service mesh.
How will your presentation benefit the e: Implementing a Zero Trust architecture usually sounds great on paper but falls apart in production due to the sheer operational tax of managing sidecars and application-level logic. By shifting to Istio’s Ambient Mode, we can finally decouple security from the developer’s sprint backlog and enforce cryptographically verifiable identities at the platform layer. This talk moves past the high-level slides and dives into the actual plumbing, showing how Ztunnel handles the mTLS handshake and how Waypoint proxies enable fine-grained L7 authorization to stop lateral movement dead. The goal is to give the community a practical, incremental blueprint for containing the blast radius of a breach without nuking cluster performance or developer velocity.

Title: AI Can't Teach You Jiu-Jitsu: Developing Your Craft in the Age of AI
Description: BJJ and software engineering share a truth: real expertise can't be shortcut. Just as grapplers master technique through mat time, failure, and mentorship and not just videos, engineers must build understanding through hands-on experience, not AI-generated code. This talk maps BJJ's belt progression onto engineering career growth, explores why pattern-matching fails against novel problems, and argues that while AI is a powerful tool, dependency on it is a trap. Get on the mat. Break things.
How will your presentation benefit the e:
The Kubernetes and open source cloud computing ecosystem depends on a pipeline of engineers who don't just *use* the tools, they understand them deeply enough to contribute to them, debug them under pressure, and make sound architectural decisions with them. 

That pipeline is at risk.

As AI coding assistants become standard practice, there is a growing temptation, especially among early-career engineers, to generate working Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Terraform configs, and Go code without developing the foundational understanding of why those solutions work. This talk directly addresses that risk.
Using the lens of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu belt progression as an analogy for engineering career development, this talk will challenge practitioners at all levels to think honestly about whether they are getting good or "just winning" by shipping configurations and code they can't debug, extend, or defend when something goes wrong in production.
For a community built on open source contribution, peer review, and collective ownership of complex distributed systems, this distinction matters enormously. The engineers who sustain and advance projects like Kubernetes, Argo, Cilium, and the broader CNCF landscape are the ones who earned their expertise the hard way: through real failure, mentorship, and deliberate practice. This talk makes the case for protecting and continuing that culture, even as AI tools become increasingly capable.
Attendees will leave with a sharper mental model for how to use AI as a force multiplier without becoming dependent on it, and a renewed appreciation for the mentorship, community, and mat time that the open source ecosystem has always run on.

Title: Uncovered: The Hard Truth About OpenTelemetry's Vendor Neutrality
Description: We still hear people saying, "OpenTelemetry is vendor neutral so you can switch vendors any time you want to." This is like saying that because the vCard format exists, it's easy to switch from iOS to Android. Sure, your core data will ultimately be portable, but you'll be missing a *lot* of other things.
How will your presentation benefit the e:
Tool choices can shift with reorganizations or mergers. The fact that OpenTelemetry (OTel) is vendor neutral is a superpower…but what exactly does that vendor neutrality actually mean?

OTel is designed such that even if you want to swap out OTel’s official SDK for your own, you still can, without breaking anything, as long as you implement the API. The OTel Collector is designed so that you can ingest telemetry data from multiple data sources and multiple formats, and export data using OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol) to any OTLP-compatible backend.

The ability to mix-and-match OTel-compatible tools, and to pick and choose pieces of OpenTelemetry to adopt, means that build-vs-buy is no longer a binary choice, but a spectrum of choice. End-users are empowered to leverage multiple tools simultaneously, if that best suits their needs. Vendors are empowered to provide ergonomic enhancements on top of open standards. 

OpenTelemetry is vendor neutral on data ingest. This means that you can point your OTel Collector to two or more OTel-compatible backends. But once the data is ingested…
Not all backends may support all 3 “main” OTools may visualize OTel signals differently
Dashboards and dashboard query languages vary across tools. For example, some use PromQL, some use their own proprietary query language, and some use SQL.
Some tools optimize on structuring OTel data differently, which can affect pricing when switching to another tool. For example, some vendors encourage sampling. Some discourage sampling. Some encourage enhancing traces with attributes. Some may encourage adding span events to traces.
The power of choice means that users can assemble the solution that works for them in pursuit of Observability's true promise: the ability to ask useful questions, get meaningful answers, and enable practitioners to act effectively on what they’ve learned.

This talk will unpack OpenTelemetry’s vendor neutrality, and help decision makers and practitioners alike understand what’s truly vendor-neutral and what’s not, helping them select the right tools for their own purposes, and to help them avoid those nasty surprises that come in the form of giant bills, giant learning curves, and interminable migration timelines.

Title: Open Source Didn't Build Itself: Community Is the Real Infrastructure
Description:

In this talk, I challenge the community to treat the open source community health with the same rigor we apply to our infrastructure, as a call to action for every practitioner in the room to move from consumer to contributor.
How will your presentation benefit the e: This talk addresses a crisis hiding in plain sight: 60% of open source maintainers are ready to quit, yet most practitioners consume without contributing. By reframing contribution as infrastructure maintenance, not charity, it shifts behavior at scale, protects the software supply chain, and plants seeds that ripple outward through the entire KCD organizer network. No tool, chart, or sponsor can fix human motivation.
